newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends weaker as stocks slide, US trade gap grows.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends weaker as stocks slide, US trade gap grows.

text.p: The dollar ended slightly weaker against the mark and yen Friday, hurt by a sharp slide in the U.S. stock market and government data that showed the U.S. trade deficit widened in May.
The Commerce Department reported that the trade gap in goods and services flared to a larger-than-expected $10.23 billion during the month, up from $8.75 billion in April.

The report also showed that the politically sensitive bilateral deficit with Japan shrank by 25 percent in May to $3.63 billion, but traders used the higher overall deficit figure as an excuse to lock in profits ahead of the weekend.
A sharp tumble in the Dow Jones industrial average, which fell over 140 points at its lowpoint, and ended the day down 130.31 points at 7890.46, also weighed on the dollar.
Nonetheless, traders were confident that the dollar, supported by a strong U.S. economic backdrop, could resume its upward trajectory next week.

"The drop in the Dow did happen to impact sentiment and aid in selling the dollar off," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president of foreign exchange sales at Credit Agricole Indosuez. "But the fundamentals are still working in the dollar's favour."
The dollar ended at 115.47 yen, down from 116.07 Thursday. It slipped slightly to 1.7910 marks from 1.7941 at Thursday's close.
Keeping the dollar's losses against the mark in check were remarks from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who said that the dollar's recent strength against the mark was not "earth shaking."
The comments followed similar remarks from Hans-Juergen Krupp, a member of the German central bank's policymaking council, who said Thursday that the dollar's rise was "nothing spectacular."
They relieved fears that Germany could soon intervene to prop up its ailing currency and pushed the dollar briefly above the 1.80 mark threshold.
However, it's failure to stay above that key psychological hurdle for a fourth consecutive day weighed on sentiment and ultimately contributed to the dollar's weakness.

"People were looking for the dollar to hold above 1.80 marks and we did not do that," said Tarek Sherlala, a foreign exchange dealer at Arab Banking Corp. "So people decided they should take whatever profits they made earlier in the week."
In other trade on Friday, the dollar fell to 1.4760 Swiss francs from 1.4828 on Thursday and ended lower at Canadian $1.3748 against $1.3768. The British pound rose to $1.6805 from $1.6722.
